Filtering: places, dates and storms

Source: vignettes/filtering.Rmd
filtering.Rmd
library(gtropic)

gtropic_data() has three ways to filter queries: by geography, temporality, and by specific storms. There is just one rule governing how the different filters can combine. This vignette covers the rule, each type of filter, and a worked example.

The combination rule

Values within a single argument are combined with a logical “OR” (union). Values across different arguments are combined with a logical “AND” (intersection).

This is the same rule as in dplyr::filter(), or SQL’s WHERE clause.

# Within a single argument implies a union (OR). E.g., Every unit in the United States OR Mexico
gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = c("United States", "Mexico"))

# Across arguments implies an intersection (AND). E.g., Units named "San Jose" that are ALSO in Costa Rica
gtropic_data(ADM2_NAME = "San Jose", ADM2_GROUP = "CRI")

The second query returns all G-TROPIC data for one ADM2 unit, not every San Jose in the world plus every Costa Rican unit. Another example:

# Across arguments implies an intersection (AND), e.g. Hurrican Katrina (2005)'s USA rows only
gtropic_data(STORM_NAME = "Katrina-2005", WHO_ENTITY = "United States")

If two arguments conflict so that nothing satisfies both, you get an error naming the arguments involved. For example:

gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = "Mexico", ADM2_GROUP = "USA")
#> Downloading 'metadata/adm2.parquet'.
#> Error in `assemble_gtropic_data()` at gtropic/R/gtropic_data.R:307:3:
#> ! No ADM2 units satisfy all of the geographic filters supplied.
#> ✖ Filters in play: `ADM2_GROUP` and `WHO_ENTITY`.
#> ℹ Values are combined with OR within an argument and AND across arguments, so these conditions must hold together.
#> ℹ Use `gtropic_adm2()` to explore valid combinations.

Geographic filters

Five named arguments select administrative units, plus polygon for spatial selection.

Argument Matches Case
ADM2_ID unit identifier exact
ADM2_NAME unit name case-insensitive
ADM2_GROUP country grouping code case-insensitive
WHO_ENTITY WHO entity, usually a country case-insensitive
WHO_REGION WHO region code case-insensitive

Names are matched case-insensitively and with surrounding whitespace trimmed; the canonical spelling from the dataset is what will appear in the resulting tables. Identifiers, on the other hand, are matched exactly.

Values that fail to match anything throw errors, including a partial miss. For example, if you supply five country names but one of them is misspelled, the whole query will fail. The error will suggest near matches:

gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = c("Untied States", "Mexcio"), date_range = c(2005, 2005))
#> Downloading 'metadata/adm2.parquet'.
#> Error in `assemble_gtropic_data()` at gtropic/R/gtropic_data.R:307:3:
#> ! 2 values in `WHO_ENTITY` did not match any ADM2 unit.
#> ✖ "Untied States" - did you mean "United States"?
#> ✖ "Mexcio" - did you mean "Mexico"?
#> ℹ See `gtropic_adm2()` for the full list of valid values.

You can use gtropic_adm2() to browse the vocabulary before querying:

gtropic_adm2()
#> # A tibble: 49,349 × 5
#>    ADM2_ID                 ADM2_NAME    ADM2_GROUP WHO_ENTITY  WHO_REGION

Filtering with a polygon

The polygon argument in gtropic_data() takes an sf or sfc object. An administrative unit is included when its population-weighted centroid falls inside the polygon. This requires the optional sf and sfarrow packages.

library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.13.0, GDAL 3.8.5, PROJ 9.5.1; sf_use_s2() is TRUE

north_carolina <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
nc_10to11 <- gtropic_data(polygon = north_carolina, date_range = c(2010, 2011))
#> Downloading 'metadata/adm2.parquet'.
#> Downloading '01_pop/2010.parquet'.
#> Downloading '01_pop/2011.parquet'.

There are two important points to keep in mind:

  1. The polygon must carry a coordinate reference system. Without one there is no way for gtropic to know what its coordinates mean, and an error will be thrown. By default a polygon in any other CRS is silently transformed to EPSG:4326 to match the published centroids. Setting reproject = FALSE turns that transformation off, which means a non-4326 input polygon will throw an error instead.

  2. Polygon membership can change between years. Population-weighted centroids move as populations shift, so a unit whose centroid sits near the boundary may fall inside the polygon in some years and outside in others. The rule is inclusive: a unit is included if its centroid fell inside the polygon in any year your query spans. The package warns whenever a polygon query covers more than one year, and warns again, listing the units, if membership actually varied. The complete list is always available:

gtropic_warnings(nc_10to11)$polygon_inconsistent
#> NULL

The named geographic filters are not year-varying, so they raise no such warning.

Temporal filters

The date_range argument takes two endpoints; Alternatively, you can use date_list, which takes a vector of specific dates. The two arguments cannot be combined.

What counts as a date

Partial dates are expanded to the start of their period for the first element of a range and the end for the second, so c(2001, 2003) covers all three years:

You write Start becomes End becomes
"2001" or 2001 2001-01-01 2001-12-31
"2001-03" 2001-03-01 2001-03-31
"2001-03-04" as given as given
a Date or POSIXct as given as given 
gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = "Philippines", date_range = c(2013, 2014))
gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = "Philippines", date_range = c("2013-11", "2013-12"))

When the order is not obvious

If your dates are not written in ISO order, the package works out the order for you, jointly, across every value you supplied rather than one at a time. That distinction matters:

# On its own "01/04/2001" could be 4 January or 1 April. But 19 cannot be a
# month, so day-month-year is impossible for this pair, which forces a
# month-day-year interpretation for both.
gtropic_storms(date_range = c("01/04/2001", "05/19/2001"))
#> # A tibble: 13 × 4
#>    STORM_ID      STORM_NAME    USA_ATCF_ID STORM_GENESIS_DATE_UTC
#>    <chr>         <chr>         <chr>       <date>                
#>  1 2001028S15128 Terri-2001    SH072001    2001-01-27            
#>  2 2001039S11139 Winsome-2001  SH082001    2001-02-08            
#>  3 2001039S13117 Vincent-2001  SH092001    2001-02-07            
#>  4 2001047N09134 Unnamed-2001  WP012001    2001-02-16            
#>  5 2001054S15155 Abigail-2001  SH122001    2001-02-23            
#>  6 2001056S11163 Paula-2001    SH132001    2001-02-25            
#>  7 2001064S10052 Dera-2001     SH152001    2001-03-04            
#>  8 2001091S11111 Walter-2001   SH172001    2001-04-01            
#>  9 2001093S10062 Evariste-2001 SH182001    2001-04-02            
#> 10 2001094S12172 Sose-2001     SH192001    2001-04-03            
#> 11 2001106N04138 Unnamed-2001  WP022001    2001-04-16            
#> 12 2001106S08137 Alistair-2001 SH202001    2001-04-15            
#> 13 2001125N05129 Cimaron-2001  WP032001    2001-05-05

When more than one interpretation of the supplied dates is possible, gtropic will pick by precedence – ymd, then mdy, then dmy – before issuing a warning, naming both the interpretation chosen and the one rejected:

gtropic_storms(date_range = c("01/04/2001", "05/06/2001"))
#> Warning: Dates "01/04/2001" and "05/06/2001" are ambiguous.
#> ℹ Interpreting as "mdy", so "01/04/2001" means "2001-01-04".
#> ℹ Rejected alternative: "dmy".
#> ℹ Set `date_format` to be explicit, e.g. `date_format = "dmy"`.
#> # A tibble: 13 × 4
#>    STORM_ID      STORM_NAME    USA_ATCF_ID STORM_GENESIS_DATE_UTC
#>    <chr>         <chr>         <chr>       <date>                
#>  1 2001028S15128 Terri-2001    SH072001    2001-01-27            
#>  2 2001039S11139 Winsome-2001  SH082001    2001-02-08            
#>  3 2001039S13117 Vincent-2001  SH092001    2001-02-07            
#>  4 2001047N09134 Unnamed-2001  WP012001    2001-02-16            
#>  5 2001054S15155 Abigail-2001  SH122001    2001-02-23            
#>  6 2001056S11163 Paula-2001    SH132001    2001-02-25            
#>  7 2001064S10052 Dera-2001     SH152001    2001-03-04            
#>  8 2001091S11111 Walter-2001   SH172001    2001-04-01            
#>  9 2001093S10062 Evariste-2001 SH182001    2001-04-02            
#> 10 2001094S12172 Sose-2001     SH192001    2001-04-03            
#> 11 2001106N04138 Unnamed-2001  WP022001    2001-04-16            
#> 12 2001106S08137 Alistair-2001 SH202001    2001-04-15            
#> 13 2001125N05129 Cimaron-2001  WP032001    2001-05-05

Supplying date_format skips inference entirely and silences the warning:

gtropic_storms(date_range = c("01/04/2001", "05/06/2001"), date_format = "dmy")

If none of the above interpretations work, you get an error showing the offending strings.

Storms are selected by their genesis date

Importantly, date_range and date_list select storms whose STORM_GENESIS_DATE_UTC falls within the requested period, i.e. the UTC calendar date of a storm’s first best-track observation, which is when it formed, not when it made landfall, and not when it began to impact ADM2s. In this way, all data for these storms is then returned, subject to your other filters. There are two consequences to this approach:

  1. This will retrieve exposure data that may fall outside the requested range, provided it is associated with a storm whose STORM_GENESIS_DATE_UTC is within the range. E.g., A storm forming on 30 September that persists for ten days contributes exposure and rainfall rows well into October. If you ask for all data associated with the storms beginning in September, those October rows will be retrieved as well, even though your range ended on 30 September.

  2. A storm that formed before your range is excluded entirely, even if it struck your region inside the range. E.g., a storm forming on 28 August that hits Texas on 3 September would not be returned by:

gtropic_data(ADM2_GROUP = "USA", date_range = c("2002-09-01", "2002-09-30"))

That is an expected exclusion of a Texas storm, and if you are studying September hospital admissions, you will want to expand your date range accordingly.

Why does the temporal filter use storm genesis date?

Because genesis is a property of the storm rather than of any place it visited, date_range selects the same set of storms every time, whatever geographic filters accompany it. Two collaborators studying Florida and Cuba over the same period are working from the same storm list, and can compare results directly. Selecting by exposure date instead would give each of them a different storm set.

How to retrieve storms by when they impacted an ADM2

Query a generous range and filter the returned links table on LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST, which is the local date the storm passed closest to each unit:

library(dplyr)

# Widen by a couple months at each end to catch storms that formed before September
res <- gtropic_data(
  ADM2_GROUP = "USA",
  date_range = c("2002-07-01", "2002-11-30")
)

struck_in_september <- res$links |>
  filter(
    LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST >= as.Date("2002-09-01"),
    LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST <= as.Date("2002-09-30")
  )

How far to widen is a judgement call: tropical cyclones rarely persist beyond two or three weeks, so two months either side is generous.

Storm filters

Three arguments select storms directly. STORM_NAME is matched case-insensitively; STORM_ID and USA_ATCF_ID must match exactly.

gtropic_data(STORM_NAME = "Haiyan", date_range = 2013)
gtropic_data(USA_ATCF_ID = "WP312013")

Storm names repeat across basins and years, so pairing a name with a date range is usually what you want. gtropic_storms() disambiguates:

gtropic_storms(STORM_NAME = "Haiyan")
#> Error in `gtropic_storms()`:
#> ! 1 value in `STORM_NAME` did not match any storm.
#> ✖ "Haiyan" - no close match found
#> ℹ See `gtropic_storms()` for the full list of valid values.

Worked example: an exposure cohort

Suppose you are estimating the effect of cyclone exposure on hospital admissions in the Philippines over 2013-2015, and you need an exposure table keyed by administrative unit and date.

library(dplyr)

phl <- gtropic_data(
  WHO_ENTITY = "Philippines",
  date_range = c(2013, 2015),
  tables = c("wind", "precip", "pop", "adm2")
)

Start from the pairs. Every unit-storm pair the dataset evaluated is in links, including pairs with no measurable wind, which matters here: a unit that got heavy rain but no wind is still exposed.

exposure <- phl$links |>
  select(ADM2_ID, STORM_ID, LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST, STORM_DIST_KM,
         WIND_EXPOSURE)

# How many units did each storm reach, and how closely?
exposure |>
  group_by(STORM_ID) |>
  summarise(
    units = n(),
    with_wind = sum(WIND_EXPOSURE),
    nearest_km = min(STORM_DIST_KM)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(units))

Attach the wind measurements, and population so you can express exposure per capita:

cohort <- exposure |>
  left_join(phl$wind, by = c("ADM2_ID", "STORM_ID")) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(format(LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST, "%Y"))) |>
  left_join(
    phl$pop |> select(ADM2_ID, YEAR, POP_TOTAL),
    by = c("ADM2_ID", "year" = "YEAR")
  ) |>
  left_join(
    phl$adm2 |> select(ADM2_ID, ADM2_NAME),
    by = "ADM2_ID"
  )

Note the population join is on year as well as unit: population changes, and using a single year’s figures across a multi-year study would bias any per capita rate.

For rainfall, do not join precip to links naively – one rainy day can fall inside two storms’ windows, and joining without care will count it twice. The linkage vignette shows how to do it properly.

Finally, record what you used:

saveRDS(gtropic_manifest(phl), "phl-2013-2015-manifest.rds")
